Unit 02 · Chapter 2

Linear Regression

CSE 30124 · Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
William Theisen · University of Notre Dame
Linear Regression01

Classification and regression

Our previous models, k-Nearest Neighbors and Decision Trees, were built for classification.

A classification task is one in which we try to assign a label (class) to a sample.

In regression tasks, we try and assign a continuous value to each sample.

Regression is another form of supervised learning.

Quick check (old exam question): is a regression task supervised or unsupervised learning?
Supervised: every training sample comes with the true target value, so we can measure how far off each prediction is.
Show answer

Supervised: every training sample comes with the true target value, so we can measure how far off each prediction is.

Linear Regression · Regression02

Why not just use classes?

How many points will Notre Dame score on Saturday? We could force that into a classification problem, with one class for 0 to 10 points, one for 11 to 20, and so on, and hand it to a decision tree. It would technically work.

Unfortunately, it throws away the order of the answers. To a classifier the classes are just labels, so guessing 11 to 20 when the answer was 21 to 30 is exactly as wrong as guessing 41 to 50. There also isn't a short list of right answers to begin with, 27 and 28 are both perfectly reasonable guesses. What we actually want is a model that hands back a number.

Linear Regression · Regression03

Linear regression

A linear regression is a technique to fit a line to our data, allowing us to make predictions.

Regression vocabulary

Unfortunately, because linear regression is so old, it has a lot of vocab specific to it:

\lk{yhat}{\yhat} = \lk{slope}{w_1 x_1} + \lk{w0}{w_0}
1
2
3
4
5
6
def predict(x1, w0, w1):
slope = w1 * x1
return slope + w0
# 400 yards (x1 = 4), with w0 = -6.7 and w1 = 9.0
print(predict(4, -6.7, 9.0))
Output
29.3
  • ŷ: the prediction (predicted target)
  • w1, w0: the weights: slope and intercept (bias)
  • x1: the input feature

Note: statistics books write these weights as β1 and β0. We use w, and it's the letter we'll use for weights in every model from here on.

Running example. All the way through this chapter we'll be trying to answer one question: how many points will Notre Dame score, given how many yards it gains? We have the box score of every Notre Dame game from 2012 to 2022, 141 games in all. Our input feature x1 is Notre Dame's total yards in a game, measured in hundreds of yards (so a 450-yard game is x1 = 4.5), the target y is the points it scored and ŷ is our model's guess. The slope w1 is then "points per 100 yards", and the intercept w0 is what the line predicts for a game with no yards at all.

Linear Regression · Regression04

Why a line?

A line is about the simplest model there is. It takes in a number and hands back a number, and it only has two knobs to turn: the slope, how much our prediction moves when the input moves, and the intercept, where the line starts. Two knobs also means we can look at a fitted line and say exactly what it learned, which is more than we'll be able to say for most of the models later on.

It's also extremely old. Legendre published the method of least squares in 1805. Gauss then claimed he'd been using it since 1795 to track the orbits of planets, he just hadn't gotten around to publishing it. The two of them argued about it for years, and astronomers, statisticians and economists have all been fitting lines (and inventing their own words for the parts) ever since.

Linear Regression · Regression05

Matrix notation

We can represent basically everything as matrices and matrix operations. Put a 1 at the front of every sample, xi = [1, xi1], and put the weights in one row, w = [w0, w1]. Then a prediction is one dot product, and stacking the samples as the rows of X predicts all of them at once:

\lk{yhat}{\yhat} = \lk{X}{X}\,\lk{w}{w\T}
Step 1 of 1: every prediction at once

Each row of X is one game: a 1 (for the intercept) and its yards in hundreds.

import numpy as np
X = np.array([[1, 2], [1, 3], [1, 4], [1, 5], [1, 6]])
w = np.array([-5.2, 9.0]) # [w0, w1]

Linear Regression · Regression06

Multiple features

It's rare that we have datasets with only a single feature. The iris dataset, a toy dataset, has 4!

When we perform a linear regression on a dataset with more than one feature, we call this a multiple linear regression.

Hyperplanes

With one feature the model is a line, with two it's a plane and with more it's a hyperplane.

Quick check (old exam question): what would the equation look like for a multiple linear regression with three features?
ŷ = w1 x1 + w2 x2 + w3 x3 + w0: one weight per feature, plus the intercept.
Show answer

ŷ = w1 x1 + w2 x2 + w3 x3 + w0: one weight per feature, plus the intercept.

A hyperplane is just a flat surface one dimension smaller than the space it lives in (a line in 2D, a plane in 3D, and past that we can't draw it but the math doesn't care). Each weight still means how much ŷ moves when that one feature goes up by 1 and everything else stays put.

Linear Regression · Regression07

Two features: yards and turnovers

Back to football. A box score has a lot more in it than just yards, so let's give our model a second feature, x2, Notre Dame's turnovers. Fitting to all 141 games we get:

\yhat = 8.8\,x_1 - 2.7\,x_2 - 2.3

Each weight now answers a "holding everything else still" question. If yards stay the same, every turnover costs Notre Dame about 2.7 points. Notice that the yards weight barely moved (9.0 alone, 8.8 here), turnovers are telling the model something yards didn't. The line on its own explained 55% of the game-to-game variation in points, the plane explains 62%. (This "fraction of the variation explained" has a name, R², so the line has R² = 0.55 and the plane R² = 0.62.)

More features isn't always more information. If we swap turnovers for first downs instead, the first-downs weight comes out almost exactly 0 and the fit doesn't improve at all. Teams that gain a lot of yards also pick up a lot of first downs, so once yards is in the model first downs has nothing new to tell it.

Linear Regression · Regression08

Fitting our line

How do we actually find the line that "fits" the best?

Live: open the football data in the visualizer, then drag the line yourself and watch the MSE.

Every one of these lines misses most of the games. The dotted segments are the misses, called residuals, yi − ŷi. The line that's too flat under-predicts the big games and over-predicts the small ones, and the line that's too steep does the reverse. If we want to call one line the "best" we need a single number that sums up all 141 misses.

Linear Regression · Fitting the line09

Optimization problems

We need some way to measure how well our model fits our data. We can call this a loss function.

For linear regression we often use SSE or MSE.

\text{SSE}(w) = \lk{sum}{\sum_i} \lk{sq}{(\lk{err}{y_i - \lk{yhat}{\yhat_i}})^2} \text{MSE}(w) = \lk{mean}{\frac{1}{n}\sum_i} (y_i - \yhat_i)^2
1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8
9
import numpy as np
x = np.array([2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
y = np.array([14, 20, 31, 40, 49])
y_hat = 9.0 * x - 5.2
sse = np.sum((y - y_hat) ** 2)
mse = np.mean((y - y_hat) ** 2)
print(round(sse, 2), round(mse, 2))
Output
4.8 0.96
Linear Regression · Fitting the line10

Why squared errors?

Why square the errors? If we just added up our residuals, a game we over-predicted by 10 points and a game we under-predicted by 10 points would cancel out, and a truly terrible line could end up with a total error of 0. Squaring makes every miss count against us.

It also means big misses are punished much more than small ones (being off by 20 points costs 400, being off by 2 costs only 4). Our line will try extremely hard not to be badly wrong about any single game, which is great until there's one truly bizarre game in the data, at which point the whole line gets dragged toward it. Unfortunately, college football has a lot of bizarre games.

The last reason is less exciting but probably the most important: a square is smooth, so we can take its derivative. We'll be doing exactly that in a page or two.

MSE is just SSE divided by the number of samples, n. Dividing everything by the same number doesn't move the bottom of the bowl, so both pick the same line. For our football line the MSE is about 70, which works out to a typical miss of about 8 points (√70 ≈ 8.4).

Linear Regression · Fitting the line11

Finding our weights

So given a loss function, our goal is to minimize it.

When would a loss function be minimized? When the gradient is zero.

Visualizing loss

We can plot the loss function with respect to w:

This bowl is a parabola because SSE is a sum of squares of things that are linear in w. A bowl has exactly one lowest point, and at that point the slope is flat.

A shape like this is called convex, and that's extremely good news for us. There's no false bottom to get stuck in, so wherever the slope is zero is the best answer, not just a pretty good one. (The one catch is when XT X has no inverse, which we'll run into in a few pages. Then the bottom is a flat valley and lots of weights tie for best.)

Linear Regression · Fitting the line12

One weight first

Before we do this with matrices, let's do it with a single weight. Take the five games from the worked example a couple of pages on, and leave out the intercept entirely so our line is just ŷ = w1 x (it has to go through 0, which is why the answer below comes out 7.8 instead of 9.0). Now the loss only has one knob, and we can take a regular derivative:

\text{SSE}(w_1) = \sum_i (y_i - w_1 x_i)^2 \text{take the derivative and set it to } 0 -2 \sum_i x_i (y_i - w_1 x_i) = 0 \text{solve for } w_1 w_1 = \frac{\lk{sxy}{\sum_i x_i y_i}}{\lk{sxx}{\sum_i x_i^2}} \approx 7.8
1
2
3
4

import numpy as np
x = np.array([2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
y = np.array([14, 20, 31, 40, 49])
# set the derivative to 0 and solve for w1
w1 = np.sum(x * y) / np.sum(x * x)
print(np.sum(x * y), np.sum(x * x), round(w1, 2))
Output
706 90 7.84

With two weights we do exactly the same thing twice, once per weight, and both derivatives have to be zero at the same time. A list of derivatives like that, one per weight, is called the gradient. One more piece of notation for the next page: ‖v‖2 is the sum of the squares of the entries of v, so ‖y − X wT‖2 is the SSE of every sample at once.

Linear Regression · Fitting the line13

Ordinary least squares

We can solve for the gradient equaling 0:

L(w) = \norm{y - X w\T}^2 \text{take the gradient and set it to } 0 -2\,X\T (y - X w\T) = 0 \text{multiply out} \lk{normal}{X\T X\,w\T = X\T y} \text{multiply both sides by } (X\T X)^{-1} w\T = \lk{xtx}{(X\T X)^{-1}} \lk{xty}{X\T y}
Step 1 of 5: turn X on its side

X 5×2
→

Xᵀ 2×5
Xᵀ row 1, column 1 is X row 1, column 1: rows become columns

import numpy as np
x = np.array([2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
y = np.array([14, 20, 31, 40, 49])
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
# the normal equations: (X^T X) w = X^T y
w = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)
print(w)
Output
[-5.2  9. ]

This is called Ordinary Least Squares (OLS).

Give X a column of 1s for the intercept, then follow the OLS recipe.

X\T = \Bb{\begin{matrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \end{matrix}} \qquad y\T = \bb{\begin{matrix} 14 & 20 & 31 & 40 & 49 \end{matrix}} X\T X = \Bb{\begin{matrix} 5 & 20 \\ 20 & 90 \end{matrix}} \qquad X\T y = \Bb{\begin{matrix} 154 \\ 706 \end{matrix}} (X\T X)^{-1} = \frac{1}{50}\Bb{\begin{matrix} 90 & -20 \\ -20 & 5 \end{matrix}} w\T = \frac{1}{50}\Bb{\begin{matrix} 90\cdot154 - 20\cdot706 \\ -20\cdot154 + 5\cdot706 \end{matrix}} = \Bb{\begin{matrix} -5.2 \\ 9.0 \end{matrix}}
Linear Regression · Fitting the line15

Reading the weights

So ŷ = 9.0 x1 − 5.2: about 9 points per 100 yards.

Quick check: in 2018 Notre Dame gained 550 yards against Stanford. What does this line predict, and what is the residual if Notre Dame scored 38?
x1 = 5.5, so ŷ = 9.0 × 5.5 − 5.2 = 44.3 points. The residual is y − ŷ = 38 − 44.3 = −6.3: Notre Dame scored about 6 points fewer than its yards suggest.
Show answer

x1 = 5.5, so ŷ = 9.0 × 5.5 − 5.2 = 44.3 points. The residual is y − ŷ = 38 − 44.3 = −6.3: Notre Dame scored about 6 points fewer than its yards suggest.

Linear regression visualization

OLS on all 141 games gives ŷ = 9.0 x1 − 6.7, the same slope (these five games happen to sit pretty close to the full-data line). Be careful with the intercept though. It says a team that gains zero yards scores −6.7 points, which is obviously impossible. No game in our data is anywhere near zero yards, so the line was never asked to be right there.

Linear Regression · Fitting the line16

In code: OLS

Here's the worked example in numpy. The @ is matrix multiplication, and np.column_stack glues the column of 1s onto our x.

import numpy as np
x = np.array([2, 3, 4, 5, 6]) # hundreds of yards
y = np.array([14, 20, 31, 40, 49]) # points
# the column of 1s, then x
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
w = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y
print(w)
Output
[-5.2  9. ]

numpy hands back a plain list, so w and wT are the same thing to it. In practice we'd use np.linalg.lstsq instead of inv (it's faster and won't fall over when XT X is nearly singular), or just let sklearn do it (next page).

Linear Regression · Fitting the line18

Representing curves

How could you use a linear regression to model a sine wave?

The model only has to be linear in its weights, not in its inputs. We can hand it new features made from the old ones, like x2 or sin(x), and it still fits them with the same equation:

\yhat = w_0 + w_1 x + w_2 \sin(1.25x)

Building new features out of old ones like this is called feature engineering, and it's a lot more powerful than it looks. The catch is that someone has to know to try sin(1.25x) in the first place. When we get to SVMs we'll see a way to get huge numbers of these features almost for free, and neural networks go one step further and learn their own.

Linear Regression · Fitting the line19

A possible issue

The weight calculation relies on computing the inverse, which can be extremely computationally expensive and sometimes just literally impossible.

With d features, XT X is a (d+1) × (d+1) matrix (one row and column per weight, intercept included), and inverting it takes on the order of d3 steps, so a million features is hopeless. Worse, if one feature can be built from the others, XT X has no inverse at all.

Our football data walks straight into this. Total yards is just pass yards plus rush yards, so if we give the model all three as features, one column is the sum of the other two and XT X has no inverse. Technically ESPN's numbers disagree by 2 yards in a single game (the 2022 Gator Bowl), so the inverse does exist. It just isn't worth having. OLS hands back a weight of −64 on total yards and about +73 on both pass and rush yards (all per 100 yards). Taken at face value that says gaining yards costs you points, what's actually happening is the model latching onto one game's scorekeeping error. Funnily enough the predictions are still fine. An extra 100 passing yards adds −64 + 72 = 8 points and an extra 100 rushing yards adds −64 + 74 = 10, it's only the individual weights that have stopped meaning anything.

Linear Regression · Fitting the line20

Maximum likelihood estimation

Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) is a method of estimating the parameters of an assumed probability distribution, given some observed data.

Say we assume every game is the line plus some random noise, and that the noise follows a bell curve (a Gaussian). We can then ask which weights make the scores we actually saw the most likely. Work through the math and the log of that likelihood comes out to a constant minus SSE / 2σ2, so maximizing the likelihood is minimizing the SSE. Least squares and maximum likelihood give the exact same line, linear regression has been doing MLE this whole time.

Overfitting

Unfortunately, Linear Regressions (a form of MLE), are prone to overfitting.

Live: open the degree-8 fit in the visualizer, then remove terms or drag a point and watch the curve swing.

Linear Regression · Overfitting21

Underfitting

Underfitting is when your model is "too weak" to capture all of the underlying patterns in the data.

A straight line through the wave on page 19 is underfit: no choice of slope and intercept can follow it.

Bias and variance

The bias–variance tradeoff describes the relationship between a model's complexity, the accuracy of its predictions, and how well it can make predictions on unseen data that were not used to train the model.

Linear Regression · Overfitting22

Two ways to be wrong

There are two different ways for a model to be wrong. Bias is how wrong the model is on average because it's too rigid to follow the pattern. The straight line through the U-shaped points on page 21 is high-bias, give it a different sample of points and it will miss the curve in exactly the same way. High bias is the underfitting from page 22.

Variance is how much the model changes when the training data changes. The degree-8 curve is high-variance, move a single point and the swings near the edges flip around completely. That's overfitting, a model that has memorized the noise in its training data instead of the pattern underneath it.

Adding complexity lowers bias and raises variance, so the best model sits somewhere in the middle, at the bottom of the total-error curve. Unfortunately, training error can't tell us where that is. The degree-8 curve has the lowest training error of the three! The only way to know we've gone too far is to check the model on data it hasn't seen.

Linear Regression · Overfitting23

Checking on games we haven't seen

The standard way to do that is to hold some of the data back. We split the games into a training set, which the model gets to fit, and a test set, which it never sees until we're done. The error on the test set is our estimate of how the model will do on the next game.

For the football data the natural split is by time. We train on the 103 games from 2012 to 2019 and test on the 38 games from 2020 to 2022, which is exactly where we'd be if we had built the model before the 2020 season.

FeaturesHow manyTraining MSETest MSE
total yards16489

Linear Regression · Overfitting24

Reading the results

Training error goes down every time we add features, it has to, since a bigger model can always make the smaller model's predictions. Test error goes down once and then climbs. The last model has more features than there are training games, so it passes exactly through all 103 of them, and on the next three seasons it misses by about 38 points a game. The model with the best training error is the worst model in the table.

Even the simple models do worse on 2020 to 2022 than on the games they learned from. That's normal, a model always looks better on its own training data (and the later seasons aren't quite like the earlier ones). The winner, yards and turnovers, is also the pair LASSO picks out in the next chapter.

Unfortunately, every time we use the test set to choose between models, a little of it leaks into our choices. The usual answer is a third split, a validation set for choosing, with the test set kept back for one final check. We'll come back to this when we get to model evaluation.

The next chapter offers another way out. Ridge regression with λ = 100 takes the 119-feature model from a test MSE of 1,443 down to 94, without throwing away a single feature.

B. Design a regression equation that would be able to approximate the dataset.
Add a squared feature: ŷ = w0 + w1 x1 + w2 x12. In fact y = 4.5x12 + 2.5x1 + 2 hits all five points exactly.
Show answer

Add a squared feature: ŷ = w0 + w1 x1 + w2 x12. In fact y = 4.5x12 + 2.5x1 + 2 hits all five points exactly.

C. What role does the SSE play in linear regression? Why does it matter that our resulting parameter space is convex?
SSE is the loss we minimize to choose the weights. Because it's convex (strictly, it's the loss that's convex, not the parameter space) there are no false bottoms: any point where the gradient is zero is a best answer, so setting the gradient to zero (or walking downhill) finds the best weights, not just a local dip.
Show answer

SSE is the loss we minimize to choose the weights. Because it's convex (strictly, it's the loss that's convex, not the parameter space) there are no false bottoms: any point where the gradient is zero is a best answer, so setting the gradient to zero (or walking downhill) finds the best weights, not just a local dip.

D. Look at the x1 and x2 columns. What goes wrong if we fit ŷ = w0 + w1 x1 + w2 x2 with OLS?
The two columns are identical, so XT X has no inverse. Any pair of weights with the same w1 + w2 fits equally well, so there's no single answer. Drop one of the two columns (or regularize).
Show answer

The two columns are identical, so XT X has no inverse. Any pair of weights with the same w1 + w2 fits equally well, so there's no single answer. Drop one of the two columns (or regularize).

Linear Regression · Review27

Practice problems

All of these use the Notre Dame football data from this chapter (141 games, 2012 to 2022).

1. Units. Our line is ŷ = 9.0 x1 − 6.7 with x1 in hundreds of yards. A classmate refits it with x1 in plain yards. What happens to w1, to w0, and to the predictions?
w1 becomes 0.090 points per yard (100 times smaller), w0 stays −6.7, and every prediction (and R²) is exactly the same.
Show answer

w1 becomes 0.090 points per yard (100 times smaller), w0 stays −6.7, and every prediction (and R²) is exactly the same.

2. Reading a plane. With two features our model is ŷ = 8.8 x1 − 2.7 x2 − 2.3, where x2 is Notre Dame's turnovers. In 2014 against North Carolina, Notre Dame gained 516 yards, turned the ball over 3 times and scored 50. What does the model predict, and what is the residual? Then try the 2016 NC State game: 113 yards, 3 turnovers. What's strange about that prediction?
North Carolina: ŷ = 8.8 × 5.16 − 2.7 × 3 − 2.3 ≈ 35.0, so the residual is 50 − 35.0 = 15.0 points (the final was 50 to 43, a lot of points for everyone). NC State: ŷ ≈ −0.5 points, which is impossible. 113 yards is far below any other game in the data, so the model is extrapolating past where it was fit. That game was played in a hurricane, Notre Dame lost 10 to 3.
Show answer

North Carolina: ŷ = 8.8 × 5.16 − 2.7 × 3 − 2.3 ≈ 35.0, so the residual is 50 − 35.0 = 15.0 points (the final was 50 to 43, a lot of points for everyone). NC State: ŷ ≈ −0.5 points, which is impossible. 113 yards is far below any other game in the data, so the model is extrapolating past where it was fit. That game was played in a hurricane, Notre Dame lost 10 to 3.

3. Home field. Fitting Notre Dame's margin of victory (its points minus the opponent's) with one feature, x = 1 for a home game and 0 for an away or neutral-site game, gives ŷ = 8.7 x + 6.4 with R² = 0.06. What do w0 and w1 mean here? Does the tiny R² mean home field doesn't matter?
w0 = 6.4 is the average margin away from home, and w1 = 8.7 is how much bigger the average margin is at home (15.1 vs 6.4 points). The R² says home field explains only about 6% of the game-to-game variation in margin, most of which comes from who the opponent was and how the game went. Both are true at once: home field is worth about 9 points on average, it's just small next to everything else.

Linear Regression · Review28

Practice problems, continued

4. Too good to be true. A student predicts Notre Dame's margin of victory using two features, Notre Dame's points and the opponent's points. OLS gives weights of exactly +1 and −1 and R² = 1. What went wrong?
The margin is defined as Notre Dame's points minus the opponent's, so the model has just rediscovered that subtraction. This is called leakage: a feature contains the answer, and it can't be known before the game anyway. (To be fair, total yards aren't known before kickoff either, so our running example explains scores after the fact rather than forecasting them.)
Show answer

The margin is defined as Notre Dame's points minus the opponent's, so the model has just rediscovered that subtraction. This is called leakage: a feature contains the answer, and it can't be known before the game anyway. (To be fair, total yards aren't known before kickoff either, so our running example explains scores after the fact rather than forecasting them.)

5. Training error. On the held-out page, the 119-feature model has a training MSE of 0 and a test MSE of 1,443. Without looking at the test set, how could you have guessed it would do badly?
It has more features (119) than training games (103), so it can pass exactly through every training game no matter what the scores are. A training error of exactly 0 on noisy data like football scores means the model has fit the noise, which is overfitting.

Both are true at once: home field is worth about 9 points on average, it's just small next to everything else.

p. 2: Supervised: every training sample comes with the true target value, so we can measure how far off each prediction is.
p. 7: ŷ = w1 x1 + w2 x2 + w3 x3 + w0: one weight per feature, plus the intercept.
p. 16: x1 = 5.5, so ŷ = 9.0 × 5.5 − 5.2 = 44.3 points. The residual is y − ŷ = 38 − 44.3 = −6.3: Notre Dame scored about 6 points fewer than its yards suggest.
p. 26: High bias, underfit. The jumps in y are 16, 25, 34, 43: they grow by 9 every step, so y is quadratic and no straight line can follow it.
p. 26: Add a squared feature: ŷ = w0 + w1 x1 + w2 x12. In fact y = 4.5x12 + 2.5x1 + 2 hits all five points exactly.
p. 26: SSE is the loss we minimize to choose the weights. Because it's convex (strictly, it's the loss that's convex, not the parameter space) there are no false bottoms: any point where the gradient is zero is a best answer, so setting the gradient to zero (or walking downhill) finds the best weights, not just a local dip.
p. 26: The two columns are identical, so XT X has no inverse. Any pair of weights with the same w1 + w2 fits equally well, so there's no single answer. Drop one of the two columns (or regularize).
